discoveries.title: Why does Earth have day and night?
discoveries.summary: Earth spins once about every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the side turned away has night.
discoveries.detail: Rotation, not Earth moving closer to or farther from the Sun, produces the daily cycle.
discoveries.question: What directly produces day and night?

discoveries.title: Why do seasons change?
discoveries.summary: Earth’s tilted axis changes the angle and duration of sunlight in each hemisphere as Earth orbits the Sun.
discoveries.detail: The two hemispheres have opposite seasons because they tilt toward the Sun at different times of year.
discoveries.question: What is the main cause of seasons?

discoveries.title: Why does the Moon change shape?
discoveries.summary: Moon phases are our view of the Moon’s sunlit half as it orbits Earth.
discoveries.detail: Earth’s shadow is involved in lunar eclipses, not the usual monthly phases.
discoveries.question: What causes ordinary Moon phases?
answers: Changing illumination as the Moon orbits

discoveries.title: Why do we see the same face of the Moon?
discoveries.summary: The Moon rotates once in the same time it takes to orbit Earth, a relationship called synchronous rotation.
discoveries.detail: The far side receives sunlight too; it is not permanently dark.
discoveries.question: Does the Moon rotate?

discoveries.title: Why are lunar craters so well preserved?
discoveries.summary: The Moon has no thick atmosphere, flowing water, or active plate tectonics to erase most impact marks quickly.
discoveries.detail: Craters preserve a record of impacts across solar-system history.
discoveries.question: What most directly preserves many Moon craters?

discoveries.title: What keeps the Solar System together?
discoveries.summary: The Sun contains most of the Solar System’s mass, so its gravity strongly shapes the paths of planets, asteroids, and comets.
discoveries.detail: An orbit is forward motion continually bent by gravity.
discoveries.question: What chiefly keeps planets in orbit?

discoveries.title: How many planets orbit the Sun?
discoveries.summary: Our Solar System has eight planets, from Mercury to Neptune, alongside dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, and comets.
discoveries.detail: Planet classifications are defined by scientific criteria, not simply by size.
discoveries.question: How many planets are in the Solar System?

discoveries.title: Is the asteroid belt crowded like science fiction?
discoveries.summary: Asteroids are spread over a huge region between Mars and Jupiter; spacecraft can travel through it without weaving between rocks.
discoveries.detail: The belt is leftover material that never formed a planet.
discoveries.question: Where is the main asteroid belt?

discoveries.title: Why do comets grow tails?
discoveries.summary: Near the Sun, a comet warms and releases gas and dust. Solar radiation and the solar wind shape the material into tails.
discoveries.detail: A comet’s ion tail points generally away from the Sun.
discoveries.question: What helps shape a comet’s tail?

discoveries.title: How does the Sun shine?
discoveries.summary: In the Sun’s core, nuclear fusion joins hydrogen into helium and releases energy that moves outward as light and heat.
discoveries.detail: Fusion requires extremely high temperature and pressure.
discoveries.question: What powers the Sun?

discoveries.title: What can a star’s color tell us?
discoveries.summary: A star’s color is related to its surface temperature: hotter stars generally look bluer and cooler stars redder.
discoveries.detail: Color is one clue astronomers combine with brightness and spectra.
discoveries.question: Which stars are generally hotter?

discoveries.title: Do all stars live the same kind of life?
discoveries.summary: A star’s mass strongly affects how it changes over time and how it ends its life.
discoveries.detail: The Sun will evolve differently from a much more massive star.
discoveries.question: What most influences a star’s evolution?

discoveries.title: What is a nebula?
discoveries.summary: Nebulae are clouds of gas and dust in space. Some are places where stars form, while others are material shed by dying stars.
discoveries.detail: Their colors can reflect different gases, temperatures, and observing wavelengths.
discoveries.question: What is a nebula made of?

discoveries.title: What is a galaxy?
discoveries.summary: A galaxy is a gravity-bound collection of stars, gas, dust, planets, and other matter.
discoveries.detail: Galaxies come in spiral, elliptical, and irregular forms.
discoveries.question: What holds a galaxy together?

discoveries.title: Where is our Solar System?
discoveries.summary: The Solar System is in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy. The Sun lies in a smaller region called the Orion Spur.
discoveries.detail: The Solar System also orbits the Milky Way’s center.
discoveries.question: Which galaxy contains the Solar System?

discoveries.title: What is a black hole?
discoveries.summary: A black hole is an object with gravity so strong that, beyond its event horizon, light cannot escape.
discoveries.detail: Black holes can form in different ways; many large galaxies host supermassive ones at their centers.
discoveries.question: What cannot escape beyond a black hole’s event horizon?

discoveries.title: Would a black hole pull everything in?
discoveries.summary: At the same distance, gravity depends on mass. Replacing the Sun with a black hole of equal mass would leave planetary orbits similar, though Earth would lose sunlight.
discoveries.detail: This thought experiment separates gravity from light and heat.
discoveries.question: What determines gravity at a given distance?

discoveries.title: Why is looking into space also looking back in time?
discoveries.summary: Light travels at a finite speed, so light from distant objects began its journey before it reaches our telescopes.
discoveries.detail: The Sun’s light takes a little over eight minutes to reach Earth.
discoveries.question: Why do distant objects appear in the past?

discoveries.title: Why put telescopes in space?
discoveries.summary: Space telescopes can observe above much of Earth’s atmosphere, which absorbs or blurs some kinds of light.
discoveries.detail: Different observatories are designed for different wavelengths.
discoveries.question: What can atmosphere-free observing improve?

discoveries.title: How can rockets work in space?
discoveries.summary: A rocket pushes exhaust in one direction and moves in the opposite direction, so it does not need air to push against.
discoveries.detail: This follows conservation of momentum.
discoveries.question: Do rockets need air to work?

discoveries.title: How do spacecraft send information home?
discoveries.summary: Spacecraft use radio signals to communicate with Earth. Mission teams use networks of antennas to receive those signals.
discoveries.detail: Signals still take time to travel across the Solar System.
discoveries.question: What carries many spacecraft messages to Earth?

discoveries.title: Why is a spacesuit more than clothing?
discoveries.summary: A spacesuit provides pressure, oxygen, temperature control, and protection for an astronaut working outside a spacecraft.
discoveries.detail: Space is nearly a vacuum, so the body needs a controlled environment.
discoveries.question: What does a spacesuit provide?

discoveries.title: Why do astronauts float in orbit?
discoveries.summary: Astronauts and their spacecraft are continuously falling around Earth together, producing the feeling of weightlessness.
discoveries.detail: Gravity is still strong in low Earth orbit.
discoveries.question: Is gravity absent in low Earth orbit?

discoveries.title: What makes an aurora glow?
discoveries.summary: Charged particles from the Sun can interact with Earth’s magnetic field and atmosphere, causing gases high above the poles to glow.
discoveries.detail: Aurorae are signs of space weather interacting with Earth.
discoveries.question: Aurorae involve particles from which star?

discoveries.title: What does Earth’s atmosphere do for us?
discoveries.summary: Earth’s atmosphere supports life, shapes weather, and burns up many small incoming meteoroids before they reach the ground.
discoveries.detail: It also changes how we observe the sky from the surface.
discoveries.question: What often happens to small meteoroids in the atmosphere?

discoveries.title: What do we mean by the universe?
discoveries.summary: The universe includes all space, time, matter, and energy that we can observe and investigate.
discoveries.detail: Astronomers study it with observations, models, and measurements across many wavelengths.
discoveries.question: Which is part of the universe?

discoveries.title: Why do astronomers infer dark matter?
discoveries.summary: Its gravity helps explain motions and lensing effects that visible matter alone does not fully account for.
discoveries.detail: Dark matter is inferred from its gravitational influence, not photographed directly.
discoveries.question: How is dark matter chiefly inferred?

discoveries.title: What is an exoplanet?
discoveries.summary: An exoplanet is a planet orbiting a star other than the Sun.
discoveries.detail: NASA missions and ground observatories use several methods to find and study them.
discoveries.question: What does an exoplanet orbit?

discoveries.title: What is the solar wind?
discoveries.summary: The solar wind is a continuous outward flow of charged particles from the Sun.
discoveries.detail: It helps form the heliosphere, the Sun’s bubble of influence in interstellar space.
discoveries.question: What is the solar wind made of?

discoveries.title: Why send different missions to space?
discoveries.summary: Different questions require different tools: orbiters map, landers sample environments, and telescopes observe across light wavelengths.
discoveries.detail: Together, missions build evidence about worlds near and far.
discoveries.question: Why do missions use different tools?
